BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of people marched in central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country after the end of the year. Thousands staged a mass march through Baghdad, Iraq, on Saturday to protest a planned U.S.-Iraq security deal. The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the rally. At one point, several speakers at a podium addressed the mass of people, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English. Hazem al-Araji, a senior al-Sadr aide, told protesters their voices would be heard in America. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he said.  Watch protesters wave flags, swarm street » . "This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji exclaimed. Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration, the largest in Baghdad in several months, was largely peaceful. Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was being reviewed by the two governments. A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31, and U.S. officials are examining "contingencies" in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces deal to the country's various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week. The same official said negotiations on the pact had finished and the text was final. The official said the "final" draft calls for U.S. troops to be out of Iraqi cities by June 2009 and out of Iraq by the end of 2011 unless the Iraqis ask the United States to stay. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also "reached a compromise" on the issue of U.S. troops remaining immune from Iraqi law -- an issue that was a major hurdle in the talks. Baghdad has sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — Thousands of demonstrators filled the streets of central Baghdad on Saturday in a massive rally protesting a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of American troops beyond the end of the year. 

Organized by the political movement of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, the demonstration was the largest the capital had seen in several months. Addressing the crowd from a central stage, a series of speakers implored the Iraqi government to reject the draft agreement, with one shouting in English, “End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!”

If this voice cannot reach the Green Zone, we want everyone residing in that occupied area to join in proclaiming that Baghdad is free, free, and that America must leave!”

Demonstrators swept through several major thoroughfares, waving national flags amid clouds of dust. Despite the high tensions, the rally remained largely peaceful. *(Video footage from the scene showed protesters waving flags and crowding the streets.)*

Meanwhile, in Washington, Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell stated Thursday that a draft Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) governing the U.S. military presence had been “agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators” and was currently undergoing review by both governments.

With the U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence set to expire on December 31, American officials are preparing “contingencies” in the event the Iraqi government cannot secure approval from the country's various political factions, according to a senior Bush administration official. 

The same official confirmed that negotiations had concluded and the current text was final. Under its terms, U.S. forces would withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 2009 and complete a full departure from the country by the end of 2011, unless the Iraqi government formally requests that they stay.

Speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the talks, the official added that negotiators had “reached a compromise” regarding the legal immunity of U.S. personnel—a issue that had served as a primary sticking point in negotiations.

**Thousands Rally in Baghdad Against U.S. Security Pact as Deadline Nears**

**BAGHDAD** — Tensions mounted in the Iraqi capital on Friday as tens of thousands of demonstrators flooded the streets to voice overwhelming opposition to a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement. The massive rally, organized by the political party of influential Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, underscored the fierce public and political backlash threatening to derail a deal designed to govern the future of American military operations in the country.

Chanting anti-occupation slogans and waving Iraqi flags, protesters gathered in major thoroughfares and iconic public spaces, including Firdous Square. Demonstrators carried banners demanding an immediate and total end to the foreign military presence, warning the Iraqi government that endorsing the pact would amount to a betrayal of national sovereignty. Sadrist leaders addressing the crowd urged lawmakers to reject the deal outright, calling for a complete withdrawal of foreign forces without conditions.

The widespread demonstrations come at a crucial moment for bilateral relations. After months of intense diplomatic wrangling, American and Iraqi negotiators recently finalized the draft of the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA). The pact is intended to replace the existing United Nations mandate, which legally authorizes the presence of coalition forces in Iraq but is set to expire on December 31. The negotiated draft includes provisions requiring U.S. troops to pull back from Iraqi towns and cities by mid-2009, with a target for a complete military withdrawal by the end of 2011.

However, the prospect of any agreement that extends the stay of American forces—even under strict timelines—has met formidable resistance across Iraq’s political spectrum. Beyond the Sadrist movement, several prominent political factions and public commentators have expressed skepticism, raising concerns over lingering questions of national sovereignty, foreign troop immunity, and the authority of U.S. forces to conduct military operations.

This deep political polarization has left Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government in a precarious position, casting serious doubt on whether the Iraqi Parliament will approve the pact before time runs out. 

With the December 31 deadline looming, the mounting domestic political stalemate has forced U.S. military commanders and Pentagon officials to prepare for the worst-case scenario. American military officials have quietly begun drafting contingency plans in the event that the Iraqi government fails to ratify the agreement or request a temporary extension of the UN mandate. 

Without a valid legal framework in place by the start of the new year, American military operations would effectively be forced to grind to a halt, leaving thousands of troops in legal limbo and jeopardizing ongoing security efforts across the nation.

In January 1991, the world watched in real-time as the opening salvos of the Gulf War unfolded on live television. Millions of viewers sat transfixed in front of their screens as **CNN** reporters broadcasted from a hotel room in **Baghdad**, capturing the eerie glow of anti-aircraft fire and explosions lighting up the night sky. 

That pivotal moment marked a watershed in media history. For the first time, international audiences experienced the immediate, unfiltered reality of war as it happened. The coverage from **Iraq** not only established CNN as a dominant global news network but also gave rise to what political scientists would later call "The CNN Effect"—the phenomenon where real-time news coverage directly influences foreign policy decisions and public perception.

Twelve years later, Baghdad once again became the focal point of global attention during the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. CNN correspondents, alongside other international journalists, reported from the heart of the Iraqi capital, documenting the fall of Saddam Hussein’s regime, the chaotic aftermath, and the years of violent insurgency that followed. Journalists operating out of Baghdad faced immense risks, balancing the imperative to report the truth with the daily dangers of a war zone. 

Beyond the politics and military conflicts, the long-standing media presence in Iraq helped bring the human stories of Baghdad to light. Through the lenses of news crews, the world witnessed not just the devastation of conflict, but the resilience of the Iraqi people, the rich historical heritage of a city once known as the center of the Islamic Golden Age, and its ongoing struggle for stability and democracy.

Today, as Baghdad works toward reconstruction and economic recovery, the legacy of those historic broadcasts remains strong. The relationship between CNN and Baghdad stands as a defining chapter in the evolution of modern journalism, proving that frontline reporting has the power to bridge vast distances and bring global events directly into the living rooms of the world.

* Tens of thousands gather in Baghdad to protest proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact
* Rally organized by loyalists of nationalist Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr
* Proposed agreement sets 2011 deadline for full U.S. military withdrawal
* Current U.N. mandate authorizing foreign troops expires December 31

**(CNN)** — Tens of thousands of Iraqis flooded the streets of central Baghdad on Saturday, burning effigies of President George W. Bush and chanting anti-American slogans to protest a proposed security agreement that would govern the presence of U.S. troops in the country.

The massive demonstration, organized by loyalists of the anti-American Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, packed into Firdos Square—the same plaza where U.S. Marines famously helped tear down a statue of Saddam Hussein in 2003.

Demonstrators waved Iraqi flags, hoisted green Shiite banners, and carried signs reading "No to the pact" and "Out, out occupation." Many burned American flags and beat effigies of President Bush with shoes—a deep insult in Arab culture.

"We demand the immediate, unconditional withdrawal of all foreign forces from our sacred land," said Sheikh Abdul Hadi al- محمداوي (al-Muhammadawi), a Sadrist leader who read a statement on behalf of al-Sadr to the roaring crowd. "Signing this agreement is a betrayal of Iraqi sovereignty."

The draft pact, known as the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), is currently being debated by the Iraqi cabinet and parliament after months of tense negotiations between Washington and Baghdad. 

If approved, the deal would establish a legal framework for U.S. military operations after the current United Nations mandate expires on December 31. Under the draft terms, U.S. combat forces would withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, with a complete pullout of all American troops by the end of 2011.

Despite these timelines, critics argue the agreement leaves open loopholes that could extend the U.S. presence indefinitely and compromise Iraqi law.

"This agreement gives the Americans everything they want and leaves Iraqis with empty promises," said Ahmed al-Tamimi, a 34-year-old schoolteacher who traveled from Sadr City to join the rally. "Five years of occupation is enough. We want our country back."

The Iraqi government, led by Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, finds itself walking a fine line. Officials in Baghdad acknowledged the anger on the streets but warned that failing to reach a deal before the end of the year could leave U.S. troops without a legal mandate, potentially forcing a sudden pullout that could jeopardize recent security gains.

U.S. officials have expressed frustration with the political delays in Baghdad, emphasizing that the draft represents significant concessions from Washington, including subjecting U.S. troops and defense contractors to Iraqi legal jurisdiction under specific circumstances involving serious crimes committed off-duty and off-base.

Saturday's protest was heavily guarded by Iraqi police and military personnel, who set up vehicle checkpoints and blanketed the surrounding neighborhood to prevent potential bombings by insurgent groups. Despite the fiery rhetoric, the rally concluded without major incidents of violence, according to Baghdad police.

The draft agreement is expected to face a crucial vote in the Iraqi parliament in the coming weeks, where Sadrists and several Sunni factions have vowed to defeat it unless major amendments are made.

*CNN's Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.*

**MASSIVE SADRIST PROTESTS ERUPT IN BAGHDAD AGAINST DRAFT U.S.-IRAQ SECURITY PACT**

**Byline:** Staff Reporter  
**Dateline:** BAGHDAD — October 18, 2008  

Tens of thousands of Iraqi Shiites loyal to the nationalist anti-American cleric Muqtada al-Sadr flooded the streets of central Baghdad today, staging a massive demonstration against the proposed U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA). 

Chanting slogans against the American presence and burning effigies of U.S. President George W. Bush, the crowds converged on Firdos Square—the iconic plaza where Saddam Hussein’s statue was pulled down in 2003—to demand an immediate, unconditional withdrawal of all foreign troops and to denounce the pending security pact as an "agreement of shame."

The rally comes at a critical juncture for both Washington and Baghdad. With the United Nations mandate authorizing foreign forces in Iraq set to expire on December 31, 2008, the draft agreement is intended to provide a legal framework for American troops to remain in the country. However, the proposal has ignited fierce political resistance across Iraq's political spectrum, with the Sadrist movement spearheading opposition on the streets.

### Protesters Demand Immediate End to "Occupation"

Surrounded by a heavy perimeter of Iraqi soldiers and police, demonstrators carried Iraqi flags and black banners bearing anti-occupation slogans. Senior Sadrist leaders delivered fiery sermons to the crowd, conveying messages from Muqtada al-Sadr, who remains in self-imposed exile in Iran.

Addressing the vast assembly at Firdos Square, Hazem al-Araji, a senior Sadrist cleric and top aide to al-Sadr, delivered a scathing rejection of the security deal and urged the Iraqi parliament to vote against it.

"We say no, no to the agreement of shame and dishonor!" al-Araji shouted to cheering supporters. "We demand the immediate departure of the occupier forces without any conditions or pacts that bind Iraq to the American empire."

Al-Araji warned the government of Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki against bowing to Washington's pressure, emphasizing that no compromise on national sovereignty would be accepted by the Iraqi public. "The Iraqi people will not accept the selling out of their country under the guise of security," al-Araji said. "The blood of our martyrs will not be compromised by a signature on an agreement that protects foreign invaders."

### Key Terms of the Draft Agreement

The draft pact, negotiated over months of tense bilateral talks, sets explicit timelines for the drawdown of U.S. forces, but critics argue it grants too many concessions to Washington. 

Under the terms of the negotiated draft:
* **Troop Withdrawal Timelines:** All U.S. combat forces are required to withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages by **June 30, 2009**. Furthermore, a firm deadline is established for the complete withdrawal of all U.S. troops from Iraqi territory by **December 31, 2011**.
* **Targeting Provisions:** U.S. forces are prohibited from using Iraqi land, air, and water as a launching pad to conduct attacks against neighboring countries, such as Iran and Syria.
* **Control of Operations:** Joint military operations are to be coordinated through a combined U.S.-Iraqi committee, with Iraqi authorities assuming full control over airspace and intelligence operations over time.

The most contentious element of the negotiations, however, centers on the issue of legal immunity for U.S. military personnel and contractors—a sticking point that nearly derailed the talks.

Under a delicate **immunity compromise**, U.S. service members will retain primary legal jurisdiction for acts committed while on duty or inside U.S. military installations. However, Iraq succeeded in negotiating limited jurisdiction over American troops in the event they commit "premeditated and serious crimes" while off-duty and outside U.S. bases. A joint U.S.-Iraqi committee will be tasked with determining whether a suspect was on or off duty at the time of an alleged offense. Private military contractors, meanwhile, will fully lose their immunity and fall entirely under Iraqi judicial jurisdiction.

Despite these concessions, Sadrist leaders insist the deal still leaves loopholes that favor American personnel and undermines Iraqi judicial authority.

### Pentagon Signals Limits on Further Changes

In Washington, the Bush administration has expressed mounting frustration with the delays and political resistance in Baghdad. Pentagon officials maintain that the text represents the maximum flexibility the United States can offer without compromising the safety and legal protections of its armed forces.

Speaking at a news briefing in Washington, Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell indicated that the United States considers the negotiated draft to be largely final, warning that time is running out to ratify the agreement before the UN mandate expires at the end of the year.

"The negotiations are completed," Morrell said. "This is a good agreement. It is good for the Iraqi people; it is good for the American military. It respects Iraqi sovereignty while protecting our troops."

Addressing the political jockeying within Baghdad, Morrell signaled that Washington was reluctant to reopen negotiations on core clauses. "We believe the text that has been submitted to the Iraqi government represents the limit of what we can accommodate," he said. "The clock is ticking, and the Iraqi political leadership needs to move this forward."

Morrell noted that failing to approve the agreement or secure an extension would leave U.S. operations in Iraq without a legal foundation come January 1, 2009, potentially forcing a sudden halt to military support and training for Iraqi forces.

### High Political Stakes

The protests pose a significant challenge to Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, who must balance the demands of his American allies against intense domestic political pressures and regional influences, particularly from Iran, which strongly opposes the pact. 

While al-Maliki’s cabinet has signaled a desire to secure minor amendments to the draft text to placate domestic opposition, the Sadrist movement has made it clear that nothing short of a complete reject of the agreement will satisfy their base.

As the draft pact moves toward a anticipated vote in the Iraqi Council of Representatives in the coming weeks, the Sadrist leadership promised further mass mobilizations, threatening to turn street opposition into a major political crisis for the government.

**BAGHDAD — October 18, 2008** 

Hundreds of thousands of Iraqis poured into the streets of central Baghdad on Saturday, turning the capital into a sea of red, white, and black national flags in a massive show of defiance against a proposed security agreement that would allow U.S. troops to remain in the country past the end of the year.

The demonstration, called by the powerful anti-American cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, paralyzed major thoroughfares leading toward Firdous Square—the iconic plaza where Saddam Hussein’s statue was pulled down by U.S. Marines five years ago. Today, the anger was directed firmly at Washington.

Protesters marched shoulder-to-shoulder under a blazing autumn sun, burning American flags and chanting slogans that echoed off the concrete blast walls lining the city: *"No, no to America! No, no to the occupation!"* 

An effigy of U.S. President George W. Bush was paraded through the crowd before being beaten with shoes—a profound insult in Arab culture—and set ablaze.

### A Direct Challenge to Washington and Maliki

The rally comes at a precarious moment for both the Bush administration and Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki. With the United Nations mandate authorizing foreign military forces set to expire on December 31, negotiators from both nations have been locked in tense, months-long negotiations over a Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA). 

While the draft currently under consideration sets a deadline for a full U.S. military withdrawal by the end of 2011, al-Sadr’s political block, along with a broad swath of the Iraqi public, rejects any deal that legitimizes the foreign military presence for a single day longer.

A statement from al-Sadr, who remains in Iran studying religious jurisprudence, was read aloud to the roaring crowd by senior aide Sheikh Abdul Hadi al-Darraji. The message issued a blunt ultimatum to the Iraqi parliament: reject the pact or face widespread civil disobedience.

"Get out of our land, occupiers," the statement read. "Signing this agreement is a betrayal of the Iraqi nation and a stamp of humiliation that will haunt this government for generations."

### Anger in the Streets

For many in attendance, the protest was less about parliamentary politics and more about a deeply felt exhaustion after five years of war, sectarian bloodshed, and foreign military patrols.

"We have seen five years of raids, broken promises, and destruction," said Ahmed al-Zubaidi, 34, an unemployed father of three who traveled from the vast Shiite district of Sadr City to join the demonstration. "They told us they came to bring democracy, but they brought us chaos. We do not want a treaty with the Americans. We want our sovereignty back today, not in three years."

Women draped in black abayas waved Iraqi flags, while young men held aloft portraits of al-Sadr and his late father, a revered Grand Ayatollah assassinated during Saddam Hussein's regime.

Despite the fiery rhetoric, the rally remained largely peaceful. Iraqi police and army units lined the perimeter of the demonstration, enforcing tight security checkpoints to prevent insurgent attacks. The disciplined nature of the crowd highlighted the formidable mobilization power of the Sadrist movement, which successfully transitioned its Mahdi Army militia into a political and social force following a cease-fire declared earlier this year.

### High Stakes in the Green Zone

Across the Tigris River, inside the heavily fortified Green Zone, U.S. diplomats and Iraqi officials continued their deliberations under the shadow of the protest. Prime Minister Maliki faces a delicate balancing act: while his military still relies heavily on American air support, logistics, and intelligence, he can ill afford to alienate a deeply nationalistic electorate ahead of regional elections scheduled for early next year.

American officials have warned that without a signed agreement or an extension of the UN mandate, all U.S. military operations in Iraq would legally have to freeze on January 1, 2009.

As the afternoon sun dipped behind the skyline, leaving the smell of burning plastic and rubber hanging in the dusty air, the crowd in Firdous Square slowly began to disperse. But the message delivered to both Baghdad's political elite and Washington was unmistakable: five years after the fall of Saddam, the patience of the Iraqi street has run out.

However, Iraqi lawmakers and the public, traumatized by years of high-profile civilian casualties, abuses at Abu Ghraib prison, and the 2007 Nisour Square shooting by private contractors, are demanding that foreign troops be subject to Iraqi courts for serious crimes committed off-duty or off-base.

"No agreement can be accepted that turns our judiciary into a mockery," said Ahmed al-Massoudi, a Sadrist lawmaker attending the rally. "Granting immunity to foreign soldiers gives them a license to kill Iraqis without fear of justice. Iraq is a sovereign nation, not an American military base."

The Bush administration has insisted that maintaining jurisdiction over its troops is a non-negotiable standard for U.S. military deployments worldwide. However, the political reality in Baghdad has forced Prime Minister Maliki to demand strict revisions to the draft, including a definitive timeline for full U.S. withdrawal by the end of 2011 and significant concessions on the immunity clause.

The massive turnout in Baghdad highlights the intense domestic pressure facing the Iraqi government. While U.S. officials argue that a sudden departure of American troops could destabilize recent security gains, Sadr’s movement has threatened to resume armed resistance if a security deal is signed without severe limitations on U.S. forces.

As the UN mandate's expiration date rapidly approaches, the standoff leaves Washington and Baghdad with a narrowing window to reach a compromise—or face a legal vacuum that could force an abrupt halt to U.S. military operations across the country.

# Tens of thousands march in Baghdad against U.S. security pact

* **Demonstrators flood Firdos Square demanding an immediate U.S. withdrawal**
* **Protest organized by followers of anti-American Shia cleric Moqtada al-Sadr**
* **Iraqi government insists draft agreement sets a firm timetable for troop departure**

By **Arwa Damon** and **CNN's Baghdad Bureau**  
October 18, 2008 -- Updated 18:45 GMT (02:45 HKT)

**(CNN)** -- Tens of thousands of Iraqis flooded the streets of central Baghdad on Saturday, burning American flags and chanting anti-U.S. slogans in a massive show of opposition to a proposed security pact that would allow U.S. troops to remain in Iraq through 2011.

The demonstration, organized by the movement of fiery Shia cleric Moqtada al-Sadr, culminated at Firdos Square -- the symbolic heart of the capital where a giant statue of Saddam Hussein was pulled down by U.S. Marines and celebrating Iraqis in April 2003.

### A critical deadline

The draft Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), negotiated over months by Washington and Baghdad, would replace the current United Nations mandate governing foreign troops, which expires on December 31. 

Under the terms of the draft deal, U.S. combat troops would withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, with a full military exit from the country by December 31, 2011. It also grants Iraqi courts limited legal jurisdiction over U.S. soldiers and military contractors in cases of major crimes committed off-duty and off-base.

Despite these provisions, critics argue the agreement compromises national sovereignty and legitimizes what they view as an illegal occupation.

"Three more years is three years too long," said Ahmed Hussein, a 28-year-old teacher who marched from the Shia enclave of Sadr City to join the rally. "We do not trust American promises. They came with promises of freedom, and they gave us destruction."

### Political divides in parliament

The Iraqi government, led by Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, faces a daunting challenge in securing legislative approval for the pact. 

While Maliki's administration maintains that the agreement represents the fastest and most realistic path to ending the foreign military presence, the political divide in Iraq’s parliament remains deep.

Sunni, Shia, and Kurdish political blocs are embroiled in heated debates over the deal. Some Sunni lawmakers have voiced concerns that an early U.S. withdrawal could leave them vulnerable to Shia militias or Iranian influence, while Kurdish leaders generally favor a continued American security umbrella.

"Without this agreement, there will be a legal vacuum on January 1," an official in Prime Minister Maliki’s office told CNN on condition of anonymity. "That outcome would endanger Iraq's stability far more than the pact itself."

Security was tightly controlled across the Iraqi capital during Saturday's march, with armed police and military personnel lining the route. Despite the high tensions and fiery rhetoric, the demonstration concluded peacefully without major reports of violence.

Parliamentary debates on the draft agreement are expected to resume in the coming days as the year-end deadline approaches.
